records.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
records.summary: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. records.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
records.summary: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. records.title: London Museum’s donors and the capital’s dubious domination | Letters
records.summary: Omitting to acknowledge the generosity of private donors risks reinforcing the widespread view that ‘magisterial’ civic amenities just happen by magic, writes Beth Breeze . Plus letters from Rendel Harris and Tom Uprichard Oliver Wainwright’s extremely positive review of the “magisterial” new London Museum will encourage many to visit ( Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight, 24 November ). But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. records.summary: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. records.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
records.summary: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. records.title: Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave
records.summary: White Cube Bermondsey, London Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla , after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. records.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
records.summary: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. methodology.reliability: A official primary source/catalogue; B established newsroom or independent research; C specialist, advocacy or aggregator; D alternative commentary; E unverified social/community; U unclassified. Grade describes source class, not the truth of a specific claim.
methodology.confidence: Claim confidence is left unassessed unless an upstream collector supplies a numeric value. Source grade is not claim confidence.
methodology.corroboration: The six views reuse the existing archive. Similar stories, repeated posts, syndicated copy or multiple outlets quoting one origin are not independent corroboration. A human must inspect provenance.
methodology.geolocation: Location is shown only when supplied by the source or upstream archive. No location is inferred from a headline.
methodology.limits: This is open-source situational awareness, not intelligence agency coverage, an emergency warning service, a live market terminal or a verified threat assessment.
